title: How Computers Think
subtitle: Bits, logic, programs, the internet, robots, and what AI really is
subject: Technology

pages.h: A machine that knows only two things
p: Inside every computer, phone and game console, there is nothing but switches. Billions of them, each one either on or off. That is all. A computer cannot store the number 7, or the letter B, or the colour red. It can only hold patterns of on and off.
Each on-or-off is called a bit, short for binary digit. Write it as 1 for on and 0 for off. A bit is the smallest possible piece of information: one answer to one yes-or-no question.

Why only two? Because two is easy to get right. A switch that must be either fully on or fully off can be a bit worn, a bit noisy, a bit too warm, and still be read correctly. A switch with ten positions would make mistakes constantly. Everything clever a computer does comes from doing something simple, telling 1 from 0, billions of times a second without ever getting it wrong. This book is about how piles of yes and no become music, maps, games and machines that seem to think.
pages.cap: A switch, a wire and a bulb: on or off. Every computer is this, times a hundred billion.
pages.fact: Did you know? The word 'computer' once meant a person. Until the 1940s, computers were people, often women, who did long calculations by hand.

p: You count with ten digits, 0 to 9, because you have ten fingers. When you pass 9, you start a new column: 10. Computers count with two digits, 0 and 1, and start a new column every time they pass 1. Count in binary: 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111. Those are the numbers zero to seven.

Each column is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To read a binary number, add up the columns with a 1 in them. The binary number 1011 means one 8, no 4, one 2 and one 1: 8 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11.

With eight bits, the biggest number is 11111111, which is 255, and there are 256 different patterns in all. With 32 bits you can count past 4 billion. With 64 bits, past 18 billion billion, which is why modern computers use 64. Nothing is lost by using only two digits. It just takes more columns.
pages.cap: Eight switches, each worth double the last: 1011 0000 is 128 + 32 + 16, which is 176.

pages.h: Everything on your screen is a very long list of yes and no.
p: This page, that photo, the song playing: all of it is bits. Billions of tiny switches, flipped in the right order.

pages.h: Bytes: a library in your pocket
p: Eight bits together make a byte, and a byte is the unit most things are measured in. One byte can hold one of 256 patterns, which is enough for every letter, digit and punctuation mark on a keyboard, so a letter of plain text takes one byte. This sentence is about 40 bytes.

From there, it climbs by thousands. A kilobyte is about 1,000 bytes: a few paragraphs of text. A megabyte is a million bytes: a minute of music, or a few seconds of video, or a photo. A gigabyte is a billion: an hour of high-quality video. A terabyte is a trillion: about 250,000 photos.

A modern phone holds 128 to 1,000 gigabytes. All the text in a large city library, about a million books, is roughly 1 terabyte. The whole internet is estimated at over 100 zettabytes, which is 100 billion terabytes, and nobody knows the number precisely. The letters of one copy of your DNA would take about 750 megabytes: a couple of hundred phone photos' worth, in each of your 30 trillion cells.
pages.cap: One copy of your DNA would fit in 750 megabytes: a couple of hundred phone photos' worth.

p: Look very closely at a screen and the picture breaks into tiny squares: pixels. Each pixel is three numbers, how much red, green and blue light to show, each from 0 to 255. That is one byte per colour, three bytes per pixel. Red 255, green 255, blue 0 is bright yellow. All three at 0 is black. Three bytes give 16.7 million possible colours, more than your eyes can tell apart. A phone photo is about 12 million pixels, so 36 million bytes before squeezing.

Sound is a wave of air pressure. To store it, a computer measures the pressure 44,100 times every second and writes down each measurement as a number. Play those numbers back through a speaker fast enough and you hear the wave again, smooth to your ears.
Video is pictures, 30 or 60 per second, with sound alongside. Text, pictures, sound, maps, money: a computer does not know the difference. They are all just numbers, and numbers are just bits.
pages.cap: A sound wave, measured 44,100 times a second, becomes a long list of numbers.

pages.q: What is the binary number 101 in ordinary counting?
pages.why: The columns are worth 4, 2 and 1. A 1 in the fours column and a 1 in the ones column gives 4 plus 1, which is 5.

p: Early computers used light-bulb-like glass tubes as their switches. They were the size of your thumb, got hot and burned out every few hours. In 1947, three scientists at Bell Labs in the United States built a switch out of a crystal of a material called germanium, with no moving parts and no glowing filament. They called it a transistor. A tiny voltage on one leg lets current flow between the other two: on. Remove it: off.

Then transistors got small. Today they are made of silicon, carved by ultraviolet light into chips in patterns thinner than a virus. The chip in a new phone holds about 20 billion transistors in an area the size of your fingernail, and the largest chips hold more than 100 billion. Each one can switch on and off billions of times a second using almost no energy.
For 50 years the number of transistors on a chip doubled about every two years. That is slowing now, because the switches are only a few dozen atoms wide and cannot shrink much further.
pages.cap: The first switches glowed like this bulb. Transistors do the same job with no light, no heat, and almost no size.

p: How do switches add? Connect them so one controls another, and you get a logic gate. There are only three you need. An AND gate turns on only if both of its inputs are on. An OR gate turns on if either is on. A NOT gate flips: on becomes off, off becomes on.

Now think of adding two bits. 0 plus 0 is 0. 1 plus 0 is 1. 1 plus 1 is 10 in binary, which is 0 with a 1 carried. The answer digit is on when exactly one input is on; the carry is on when both are. That is a few gates. Chain eight of these and you can add two bytes. Add many times and you can multiply. Compare, remember, branch, repeat: every single thing a computer does is built from AND, OR and NOT, stacked billions deep.

The English mathematician George Boole worked out this logic in 1854, to describe how people reason. He never saw a computer. Eighty years later, engineers realized his algebra was exactly how switches behave.
pages.cap: Like gears, logic gates pass simple actions along: a few of them can add, millions can run a game.

pages.h: Try it: count to 31 on one hand
p: Your fingers are bits. Learn to count like a computer.
steps: Hold up one hand, fingers down. Your thumb is worth 1, index finger 2, middle finger 4, ring finger 8, little finger 16.
To show a number, raise the fingers that add up to it. Three is thumb and index (1 + 2). Five is thumb and middle (1 + 4). Ten is index and ring (2 + 8).
Count from 0 to 31 in order. Watch the thumb: it flips every step, like the last bit of a binary counter. The index finger flips every two steps.
With both hands you can count to 1,023. Challenge a friend: how fast can they read the number your fingers show?
Write a secret message by turning letters into numbers (A = 1, B = 2) and then into fingers.
pages.cap: Each finger doubles the last: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Five fingers, 32 different numbers.

p: The part of a computer that does the work is the processor, or CPU. It does one very simple loop, forever. Fetch an instruction from memory. Work out what it means. Do it. Fetch the next one. An instruction is tiny: add these two numbers, move this value there, if this is zero then jump to that instruction.

What makes it powerful is speed. A clock inside the chip ticks about 4 billion times a second, and the processor does something on nearly every tick. Four billion simple steps per second, every second, with no mistakes, adds up to playing a video, running a game and scanning for messages all at once.

Modern chips are really several processors side by side, called cores: a phone has about 6, a gaming PC 8 to 16, and the chip that draws graphics has thousands of tiny ones working together, because colouring millions of pixels is the same small job done millions of times. Heat is the limit. A chip working hard can get hotter than boiling water without its fan.
pages.cap: The clock in a processor ticks four billion times a second. This one manages once.

p: A computer has two kinds of memory, and the difference matters. The first is RAM, fast memory on chips right next to the processor. It can hand over a number in a few billionths of a second, but it holds data only as long as the power is on. Switch off, and every bit in RAM goes blank. That is why you lose unsaved work in a power cut.

The second is storage: a solid-state drive, or on older machines a spinning magnetic disk. It is slower, about a thousand times slower than RAM, but it remembers with the power off, by trapping electrons in tiny cells or flipping tiny magnets. Your photos live here.

When you open an app, the computer copies it from storage into RAM to run it, and when you save, it copies back. A phone has about 8 gigabytes of RAM and 256 gigabytes of storage. Long-term, data is fragile: discs rot, drives fail, formats die. Nobody knows how to keep digital information readable for 500 years. Paper has already done it.
pages.cap: Old hard drives store bits as tiny magnets, north or south. Solid-state drives trap electrons instead.

p: A computer with no program is a pile of switches that does nothing. A program is a list of instructions, written by a person, that tells the switches what to do and in what order. It is a recipe, except the cook is extremely fast and extremely literal. If the recipe says 'add salt' and does not say how much, the cook will not guess. It will stop, or add all the salt in the world.

People do not write in 1s and 0s. They write in programming languages that look a little like English and maths, with names like Python, JavaScript and C. A second program, a compiler, translates those words into the billions of simple instructions the processor understands.

Programs get big. A phone's operating system is tens of millions of lines of code, written by thousands of people over decades. A car has about 100 million lines. Nobody understands all of it. The whole world's software is probably the largest thing humans have ever built, and it is all recipes.
pages.cap: Like building a pyramid, a big program is thousands of small, exact steps done in the right order.

pages.q: Why do you lose unsaved work when the power goes off?
opts: The processor forgets how to count
RAM only keeps its bits while the power is on
pages.why: RAM is fast but needs power to hold its bits; storage keeps data without power, but only what you saved.

p: An algorithm is a method for solving a problem, step by step, that always works. A recipe is an algorithm. So is long division. Computers run them, but people invent them, and a clever one beats a fast computer running a dumb one.

Suppose you want to find a name in a list of a billion names in alphabetical order. The slow way is to start at the top and check each one: up to a billion checks. The clever way is the way you use a dictionary. Open to the middle. Is your name before or after? Throw away the wrong half. Open the middle of what is left. Each step halves the pile. A billion names take only 30 steps. This is called binary search.

Sorting is similar. The obvious way to sort a million numbers takes about a trillion comparisons. The best methods take about 20 million, 50,000 times fewer. The programs that find your route on a map or match your face to a photo are mostly algorithms like this, found by people, some of them centuries ago.
pages.cap: Comparing two things at a time: a good algorithm needs far fewer comparisons than you would guess.

p: On 9 September 1947, engineers at Harvard found a computer giving wrong answers. Inside one of its relays was a dead moth. They taped it into the logbook with the note 'first actual case of bug being found'. The word was already used for faults in machines, but the moth made it famous, and every mistake in a program has been a bug since.

Most bugs are not moths. They are a human writing one wrong instruction out of millions. In 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the Martian atmosphere because one team's software gave a push in pounds-force and another's expected newtons. Nobody noticed. The spacecraft, worth 125 million dollars, missed its path by about 100 kilometres.

That is why programmers spend more time testing and fixing than writing. Big programs are tested by other programs that try millions of inputs automatically. Even so, every piece of software you use has bugs in it right now. The question is never whether, only which ones matter.
pages.cap: A moth, not a butterfly, jammed a relay in 1947 and gave computer mistakes their name.

p: In the 1830s, the English inventor Charles Babbage designed a steam-powered calculating machine the size of a room, and in 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote what many call the first program for it, working out how it could compute a series of numbers. The machine was never finished; the parts were too hard to make.
In 1936, Alan Turing worked out on paper that a single simple machine, reading and writing symbols on a tape, could in principle do any calculation at all. Every computer since is that machine.

The first all-electronic general computer, ENIAC, was switched on in 1945 in Pennsylvania. It weighed 27 tonnes, filled a room of about 170 square metres, used 18,000 glass tubes and did about 5,000 additions a second. Programming it meant rewiring it by hand, a job done by six women who were the first programmers of the electronic age. Your phone does about a trillion operations a second: 200 million times faster, running on a battery, in your pocket.
pages.cap: From a room of glass tubes to a chip you can lose in the sofa.

pages.h: Your phone is millions of times faster than the computer that steered people to the Moon.
p: The Apollo guidance computer had about 4 kilobytes of working memory. One phone photo is nearly a thousand times bigger.

pages.h: The internet: chopping everything into packets
p: The internet is not a cloud. It is billions of computers and phones connected by wires, fibres and radio, agreeing on a set of rules for passing messages. The main rule is simple: everything is cut into small pieces called packets, about 1,500 bytes each, and every packet carries the address it is going to and the address it came from.

A packet leaves your phone, reaches your home router, and from there hops through a chain of bigger routers, each one looking at the address and passing it toward the right neighbour, like mail sorters who only know which direction to throw a letter. Packets from one video may take different routes and arrive out of order; your phone puts them back together. If one is lost, it asks again.

The system was designed in the 1970s to keep working if parts of it were destroyed, and that is why no one owns it or can switch it off. A packet from Toronto to Tokyo makes about 15 hops and arrives in roughly a tenth of a second.
pages.cap: Every lit window is a computer; the internet is the agreement between them.

p: Every device on the internet has a number called an IP address, like 142.250.72.14. People cannot remember those, so there is a phone book: the Domain Name System, or DNS. When you type a website name, your phone first asks a DNS server, 'what number is that?', gets the answer in a few thousandths of a second, and then sends its packets to that number. The whole lookup is invisible, and it happens before any page loads.

The old addresses had 32 bits, about 4 billion possible numbers, and the world ran out of them around 2011; there are far more than 4 billion devices now. The newer system uses 128 bits, enough to give every grain of sand on Earth billions of addresses. Both run side by side today.

Behind the names are real places. Big websites run from data centres, windowless buildings the size of several football fields, packed with hundreds of thousands of computers, humming and hot, usually built somewhere electricity is cheap.
pages.cap: Six people, six addresses: DNS is the book that turns names into numbers.

pages.h: Light under the sea, waves in the air
p: Most people think the internet travels by satellite. It does not. More than 95 percent of international data runs through fibre-optic cables lying on the sea floor: about 600 cables, 1.4 million kilometres of them. Each fibre is a glass thread thinner than a hair, and the data is pulses of laser light, flashing on and off, 1 and 0, billions of times a second. Light bounces along the inside of the glass for thousands of kilometres, with repeaters every 80 or so to boost it. A single cable can carry 200 terabits per second: every book ever written in a few seconds.

The last few metres are usually radio. Wi-Fi uses radio waves at 2.4 or 5 billion cycles a second, and a thick wall or a running microwave oven can slow it. Your phone's mobile data uses towers a few kilometres apart.
Sharks have bitten the sea cables. Ships' anchors cut several every year. Repair ships sail out, hook the cable up from 4,000 metres, and splice it by hand.
pages.cap: Under the ship's keel, a glass thread the width of a hair carries a country's internet as flashes of light.

pages.q: How does most internet data cross the ocean?
opts: Through fibre-optic cables on the sea floor
Through the air as radio waves
pages.why: Undersea cables carry over 95 percent of international traffic as pulses of light in glass fibres.

p: Packets pass through dozens of machines owned by strangers. Why can nobody read your messages? Because they are scrambled, with encryption. The padlock in your browser means every packet is turned into noise using a key, a very large number, and only the computer at the other end has the matching key to unscramble it.

The clever part is agreeing on a key without anyone listening in being able to learn it. The trick, invented in the 1970s, uses maths that is easy one way and nearly impossible backwards: multiplying two huge prime numbers takes a computer a moment, but finding which two primes made the result would take every computer on Earth longer than the age of the universe. The key can be public; the secret is in the unpicking.

That is why passwords matter and why the weak spot is almost always a person, tricked into typing one in the wrong place. The maths is solid. Quantum computers, if they get big enough, might one day crack it, so new codes are being written now, just in case.
pages.cap: A castle protects with walls; the internet protects with maths that is easy to lock and very hard to pick.

p: A robot is a computer that can sense the world and act in it. Three parts: sensors to notice (cameras, microphones, touch pads, laser rangefinders that measure distance millions of times a second), a computer to decide, and actuators, the motors and pistons that move. Take away any one part and it is not a robot. A drone with no sensors is a toy; a camera with no motors is a camera.

About 4 million robots work in factories today, welding car bodies and packing boxes, doing the same precise motion ten thousand times a day without a coffee break. Robots vacuum floors, sort parcels, pick strawberries and hold surgeons' tools steady inside patients. Six rovers have driven on Mars, taking orders from Earth that arrive up to 20 minutes late, so they must drive themselves between messages.

Most robots do not look like people. The useful shape is usually an arm, a cart or a box. Humanoid robots that walk and carry things are being tested in warehouses, and they still fall over more often than their makers admit.
pages.cap: Sense, decide, act: a robot is a loop that runs many times a second.

pages.h: Why the easy things are hard
p: Here is a puzzle. A computer beat the world chess champion in 1997. In 2016, a program beat the world's best player of Go, a game with more possible positions than there are atoms in the universe. Yet no robot can reliably fold a basket of laundry, and a two-year-old can.

The reason is that chess is hard for people but simple to describe: 64 squares, clear rules, one goal. Laundry is easy for people but almost impossible to describe: cloth bends in endless ways, every sock is different, and you use touch, sight and a lifetime of practice without thinking. The skills that feel effortless to you are the ones your brain spent millions of years of evolution perfecting. The skills that feel hard, like arithmetic, are new, and we are bad at them, so machines look clever by comparison.
Engineers call this Moravec's paradox. It is why robots are great at welding and terrible at tidying your room, and why a self-driving car is a far harder project than a chess program.
pages.cap: Lifting a known weight is easy to describe and easy for a robot. Folding a sock is neither.

p: Find out how exact a computer needs its instructions to be.
steps: Pick a partner to be the 'robot'. The robot must do exactly what you say, nothing more, and must not guess.
Put bread, a jar of jam and a butter knife on a table. Your job: give instructions to make a jam sandwich, one at a time.
Say 'put jam on the bread'. A good robot picks up the sealed jar and sets it on the loaf. You never said to open it, or to use the knife.

Start over and write every step down: 'Pick up the jar with your left hand. Twist the lid with your right hand until it comes off.' Count how many steps it takes to get a real sandwich. Most people need more than 20.
Now you know what programming feels like, and why bugs happen.
pages.cap: A computer, like a very obedient robot, does what you said, not what you meant.
pages.safe: Use a butter knife, and clean up the jam.

p: For most of computing's history, a program could only do what a person had written out step by step, like the sandwich recipe. Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a different approach: instead of writing the rules, you show the computer a very large number of examples and let it work out the rules itself. This is called machine learning.

To teach a program to spot cats, you do not describe a cat. You show it a million photos labelled 'cat' and 'not cat' and let it adjust itself, a tiny bit each time, until it mostly gets them right. Afterwards, it can spot cats in photos it has never seen. The rules it found are spread across billions of numbers inside it, and no one, not even its makers, can fully read them.

The same method, with text instead of photos, produces programs that write and answer questions, by learning which words tend to follow which. They have read more than any human could in a thousand lifetimes. They are impressive. They are also not what they look like.
pages.cap: AI programs are built from simple units that pass signals on, loosely inspired by neurons like these.

p: The programs behind modern AI are called neural networks, because they are loosely modelled on brains. Picture a huge web of simple units in layers. Each unit takes numbers from the layer before, multiplies each by its own setting, called a weight, adds them up, and passes the result on. Pixels go in one end; a guess, 'cat: 80 percent', comes out the other.

At first the weights are random and the guesses are garbage. Training is correction. Show a photo, check the guess against the label, and nudge every weight a tiny bit in the direction that would have made the guess less wrong. Repeat millions of times. Slowly, the web organizes itself: early layers start detecting edges, middle layers ears and whiskers, late layers whole cats. Nobody designed that; it emerged.
The biggest networks have hundreds of billions of weights and take months to train on tens of thousands of chips, using as much electricity as a small city. Then they can run on a phone.
pages.cap: Training is correction: the mistake rate falls as millions of tiny nudges add up.

pages.q: How does a modern AI program learn to recognize cats?
opts: A programmer writes down what a cat looks like
It adjusts billions of internal numbers after seeing many labelled examples
pages.why: Machine learning finds its own rules from examples; the rules end up spread across the network's weights, not written by anyone.

p: An AI program that writes fluent sentences can seem to understand you. Be careful. What it is doing is predicting which words are likely to come next, based on patterns in everything it read. It does not know what a cat is in the way you do; it knows which words go near 'cat'. It has no body, no memories of its own life, no feelings, and no wish for anything. When it says 'I think', that is a pattern of words too.

This leads to a known problem: it can state things that are completely false with total confidence, because 'sounds right' and 'is right' are different, and it only learned the first. Lawyers have been caught filing court papers with fake cases an AI made up. Always check.

It also copies the world it read. If the examples were unfair, the program is unfair. And it uses a great deal of electricity and water for cooling. AI is a powerful tool, like a calculator for words and pictures. It is not a person, and it is not a friend, however it sounds.
pages.cap: An AI answer is an echo of what people wrote, shaped by patterns, not by understanding.

p: The fastest computers on Earth are supercomputers: warehouses of chips wired together to act as one. The leaders, in the United States, pass an exaflop: a billion billion calculations every second. They simulate the climate decades ahead, the inside of exploding stars, and how new medicines might fold. One of them uses 30 megawatts, as much power as 20,000 homes.

The data centres that run the internet and AI are bigger still, and multiplying. In 2024 they used about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity, and that share is growing fast enough that power companies are planning new plants for them. Where to get that energy is now a serious argument.

At the strange end are quantum computers, which use atoms or tiny circuits cooled to near absolute zero as bits that can be 0 and 1 at the same time. In theory they could crack problems no ordinary computer ever could. In practice, in 2026, they are still fragile laboratory machines that make mistakes faster than they make answers. Whether that changes is open.
pages.cap: A quantum bit is an atom or a tiny circuit, kept colder than deep space, holding 0 and 1 at once.

p: Computing is young, and its biggest questions are still open. The deepest is simple to ask: can a machine understand anything, or only imitate understanding? Philosophers and scientists disagree sharply, and no one has a test that settles it.

Nobody knows how your own brain computes. It has 86 billion neurons, runs on about 20 watts, learns from a handful of examples where an AI needs millions, and nobody can say exactly how. Copying it properly is not yet possible, because the original is not understood.

Mathematicians do not know whether some problems are truly impossible to solve quickly or whether we just have not found the trick. It is called the P versus NP problem, and a million-dollar prize has waited since 2000. Nobody knows whether transistors can get much smaller, or what replaces them. Nobody knows how to keep today's files readable in 500 years. The people who will answer these are mostly still in school. Some are reading this.
pages.cap: Eighty-six billion neurons on 20 watts: the machine nobody has figured out yet.

pages.h: A computer does exactly what it is told. The hard part is saying exactly what you mean.
p: Every bug, every clever program and every strange AI answer comes from that one gap.

qs: If an AI program says something kind to you, does it mean it? Does that matter?
Computers follow instructions exactly. People do not. Which is better, and when?
Data centres use more electricity every year. Is a faster internet worth building more power plants? Who should decide?
